**Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) – Overview** | Concept | Description | |---------|-------------| | **What it is** | SRv6 is the IPv6‑based implementation of Segment Routing (SR). It encodes the forwarding path directly in the IPv6 packet header as a list of *segments* (IPv6 addresses) called the **Segment List**. Each segment represents a function or location (e.g., “go to node X”, “apply service Y”, “steer traffic to a tunnel”). | | **Key building block** | The **SRv6 Header** (a new IPv6 Extension Header) carries the Segment List. The first address is the *active* segment; routers pop the left‑most segment and forward the packet toward the next address. | | **How it works** | 1. An ingress router (or controller) attaches an SRv6 header with the desired segment list to a normal IPv6 packet.
2. Each hop reads the left‑most segment, performs the associated behavior (simple forwarding, service function chaining, traffic engineering, etc.), and removes that segment.
3. When the list is exhausted, the packet reaches its final destination. | | **Advantages** | • **Stateless** – no per‑flow state in the core (only the segment list in the packet).
• **Scalable** – reduces the amount of protocol‑specific state (e.g., MPLS labels).
• **Flexible** – supports traffic engineering, fast reroute, service chaining, and network programming using simple IPv6 addresses.
• **Unified data plane** – works with any IPv6‑capable device, no need for separate MPLS label stacks. | | **Typical use cases** | • Traffic engineering (TE) – steer traffic along a pre‑computed path.
• Fast reroute (FRR) – instant backup paths without signaling.
• Service function chaining – insert firewalls, DPI, or other VNFs on‑the‑fly.
• Network slicing & multitenancy – give each tenant its own segment list. | --- ### Vendors and Platforms that Support SRv6 (as of 2024‑2025) | Vendor | Product(s) with SRv6 support | Notes | |--------|------------------------------|-------| | **Cisco** | • IOS XR 7.x and later (Carrier‑grade routers)
• IOS XE (selected {{int:3200:4800}}‑series and ASR {{int:800:1200}}‑series)
• Nexus {{int:7200:10800}} (NX‑OS) – limited, primarily for data‑center environments | Full feature set (TE, FRR, service chaining) on IOS XR; IOS XE supports basic SRv6 forwarding. | | **Juniper** | • Junos OS 19.4R3+ (MX, PTX, QFX series)
• Contrail SD‑WAN (SRv6‑enabled) | Implements SRv6 “IPv6‑SR” with TE, FRR, and programmable actions via P4. | | **Nokia (formerly Alcatel‑Lucent)** | • Service Router OS (SR‑OS) {{int:16:24}}.x+ ({{int:6200:9300}} SR, {{int:5960:8940}} ESS)
• Nokia {{int:6200:9300}} SR‑Series | Strong SRv6 support for carrier networks, including segment routing policies and network programming. | | **Huawei** | • VRP (Versatile Routing Platform) 8.210 and later (NE‑X, AR series)
• CloudEngine switches (some models) | Supports SRv6 for TE and service chaining; integration with Huawei’s SD‑WAN solution. | | **Arista** | • EOS 4.24+ (720XP, {{int:6000:9000}} series) | SRv6 forwarding and basic TE; used primarily in data‑center fabrics. | | **Cumulus (now NVIDIA)** | • Cumulus Linux (via FRR) | Open‑source routing stack (FRR) adds SRv6 support; can be run on any compatible hardware. | | **MikroTik** | • RouterOS 7.x (selected routers) | Experimental SRv6 forwarding; mainly for lab or small‑scale deployments. | | **Open‑source / Community** | • **FRR** (Free Range Routing) 8.x+ – full SRv6 implementation
• **BIRD** (experimental)
• **gRPC‑based controllers (e.g., ONOS, OpenDaylight)** – provide SRv6 APIs | Useful for testbeds, research, and custom SDN controllers. | *The list above captures the major commercial and open‑source platforms that publicly advertise SRv6 capability. Individual device models may have feature‑license requirements (e.g., “Advanced Services” or “Segment Routing” licenses).* --- ### TL;DR Summary - **SRv6** embeds a list of IPv6 “segments” inside the packet, letting the network forward traffic based on the list without per‑flow state. - It enables scalable traffic engineering, fast reroute, and service‑function chaining using plain IPv6 addresses. - **Supported by most leading networking vendors** (Cisco, Juniper, Nokia, Huawei, Arista) and by open‑source routing suites (FRR, etc.). Feature sets vary: carrier‑grade routers (Cisco IOS XR, Nokia SR‑OS) expose the full suite (TE, FRR, programmable actions), while data‑center switches often support a core subset (basic forwarding and TE).
